headline: A chip-led rebound from last week's washout ran against slightly firmer yields, while Brent's weekly gain was a prompt-spread rebuild into Sunday's OPEC+ meeting

paragraphs.equities_rates: The week was a recovery from the 20 November washout, not a fresh advance built on easier money. The S&P 500 finished 5.6% higher at 7,297 and the PHLX Semiconductor index 9.25% higher at 9,187, but almost all of that was won in Monday's bounce from 6,910 and 8,409; chips then gave a large part of the squeeze back into Wednesday before recovering into the week's close. Taiwan's Taiex rose 9.1%, in line with the SOX. Europe and Japan also finished higher, though by less — the Stoxx 600 by 2.91% and the Nikkei by 4.03%. The VIX fell by a third, to 23.8, the same snap-back from last week's stress rather than a new low-volatility regime. Even after the rebound, the S&P is still 5.5% below its level a month earlier. Treasury yields did not underwrite the rally. The 10-year par yield ended at 4.94%, only two basis points above the prior Friday, but that modest week-on-week rise hides the path: yields eased to 4.85% by 25 November, then sold off into the close. The two-year rose six basis points to 4.69%, more than the 10-year, so the curve flattened slightly and the backup was led from the front end. Equities finishing the week higher against a firmer front end, rather than against falling yields, is the tension. The interpretation is that this was a positioning rebound after the AI-led liquidation, still sensitive to next Friday's November payrolls, which feed the December hike debate.
paragraphs.metals_fx: Gold recovered 3.5% to $3,668.5 and silver 5.2% to $43.70, after both had been sold hard into 20 November — gold from $3,918 on 13 November to $3,544. The path mirrored equities: a bounce early in the week, a fade into Wednesday (gold $3,565, silver $40.54), then a recovery into the close. Platinum was only 1.8% higher; copper barely moved, up 0.5%, and aluminium finished 2.6% lower, so the rebound was concentrated in gold and silver. That bounce happened even though the dollar index ended 0.22% firmer at 104.04 and Treasury yields did not fall. Metals also faded mid-week while the dollar was softening (the index reached 103.67 on 25 November), then recovered into the close as the dollar firmed again — they traded with risk assets, not against the dollar. The interpretation is a bounce from last week's liquidation and a return of risk appetite, not a change in the rate outlook. The same firmer-yields backdrop that capped gold earlier in November is still in place.
paragraphs.oil_gas: January Brent settled at $95.44, up 3.1% on the week, ending a three-week losing streak. January WTI slipped 0.4% to $83.08 for a fourth weekly loss, and the Brent–WTI spread widened from $9.16 to $12.36. The Brent gain was concentrated at the front of the curve: the January–February spread opened from $2.62 to $4.60 of backwardation, February rose only $0.89, and the mid and back of the curve were unchanged to slightly lower. Products did not join in — December ULSD fell 5.3% and RBOB 2.4% — so this was not a demand-led move in the complex. It reads as a prompt, seaborne risk premium being rebuilt in Brent after three weeks of liquidation. The path was not a straight line. Brent traded down to $89.37 early in the week, when the surplus narrative still dominated, then recovered through mid-week and finished at $95.44, after trading as high as $98. Kpler data put Hormuz flows at only 31% of prewar levels, and the Jazan refinery attack and an Iranian drone strike in Kuwait added to that premium. Sunday's OPEC+ meeting sets 2027 quotas from capacity assessments the Iran war has made hard to pin down. What looks priced in is near-term Gulf disruption, not a tighter deferred balance; a dovish quota outcome, or any easing in the Hormuz constraint, would test the new front-end premium first. Gas went the other way, and for a different reason. January Henry Hub had been rising into 20 November, from $3.37 at the end of October to $3.748, and then reversed, finishing 6.9% lower at $3.491 as milder US forecasts after the Thanksgiving storm cut the heating-demand bid. January TTF rose early in the week, from €88.30 to €91.47, then sold off into the close at €84.58, down 4.2% on the week. Weather, not oil's Gulf premium, set the gas tape.

basis: Week-on-week = Friday 27 November 2026 close versus Friday 20 November 2026 close. Equities, metals, FX, WTI, Henry Hub and TTF, and the official US Treasury 10-year and 2-year par yields, are from emmi-data live-data market.json generated 2026-11-27T22:32:22+01:00 (Yahoo Finance daily bars; Treasury par curve for the two official yield rows). Week-on-week percentages are that file's 1W field (7-calendar-day lookback), checked against the same file's daily OHLC bars. Brent January 2027 (BRNF27, the BZF27 front month) uses ICE settles in emmi-data curves/brent/: 92.57 on 20 Nov and 95.44 on 27 Nov; the same contract was front month on both Fridays (expiry 30 November 2026, not yet rolled). market.json BZ=F matches those settles and the +3.1% week-on-week figure. A later emmi-data futures/ Yahoo/TradingView file for 27 Nov disagreed with the Friday evening settle on Brent, WTI, Henry Hub and TTF, so those Saturday prints were not used. TTF is the January 2027 contract in market.json (88.30 on 20 Nov, 84.58 on 27 Nov); the EEX curve archive's latest official file is 26 November. The 10-year prior-Friday close of 4.92% is implied by the official series' +2 basis-point 1W change on the 4.94% close of 27 Nov (the file's yields10 chart skips 20 Nov). The mid-week 10-year low of 4.85% is the official 25 November close. The two-year prior-Friday close of 4.63% is implied by the official +6 basis-point 1W change on the 4.69% close of 27 Nov. Rewritten 28 Nov afternoon after Jerry's feedback: no publication credits in the prose; deeper walk through the week's path, market links and curve structure; 'best week in more than a year' dropped because it could not be verified from held S&P history.
